text.p: The following are key facts about Afghanistan, where the purist Islamic Taleban movement and its new ethnic Uzbek allies have taken opposition strongholds in a weekend sweep:

Population: About 17 million, of whom more than 2.4 million are nomadic tribesmen. An estimated five million Afghans lived as refugees in Pakistan and Iran during the Soviet occupation in the 1980s. Islam is the main religion. Most are Sunni Moslems but there at least one million Shi'ite Moslems.

Area: 245,665 square miles (636,270 sq km). Landlocked Afghanistan borders the Central Asian republics to the north, Iran to the west and Pakistan to the south and east. Its northeast tip touches China.
Refugees: About five million Afghans fled the country during the Soviet occupation and most of them have returned after the Mujahideen guerrillas took power in April 1992.

Capital: Kabul has been the capital of Afghanistan since 1776, with a population of 800,000 to one million. Since April 1992, when the Mujahideen captured Kabul, more than 40,000 people have lost their lives and one million people have fled the city in bitter factional fighting.
The United Nations is trying to clear some 240 minefields spread over 22 square km (13 square miles) in Kabul alone.
Currency: Afghani (fluctuating between 24,300 and 16,000 per dollar on Tuesday compared to 9,781 afghanis in November).

Economy: Afghanistan has not had a formal economy since April 1992. The infrastructure in many major cities has been destroyed in the past four-and-a-half years of factional fighting. There are severe shortages of water, food, housing and other basic necessities.

Trade: Under international law, Pakistan gave landlocked Afghanistan permission to import goods duty-free through its Karachi port. For decades, Afghan traders would drive their sealed imports up to Jalalabad or Spinboldak in Afghanistan, and then turn around some of the goods to re-enter Pakistan. But last year, Pakistan imposed restrictions on Afghan imports after a dramatic increase in the volume of turnaround goods in the previous three years.

Pakistan Central Board of Revenue estimates that about 20 billion rupees ($49 million) worth of goods were smuggled into Pakistan in fiscal 1994/95 (July-June) as compared to 11 billion rupees in 1993/94.

Landmines: Ten million landmines are scattered across more than 420 square km (160 sq miles) of Afghanistan, making it one of the most heavily mined countries in the world. Landmines have killed or maimed 400,000 Afghans.

Modern history: The country was ruled by King Zahir Shah from 1933 until 1973 when the monarchy was overthrown in a bloodless coup. Mohammad Daoud, the king's cousin, became the country's first president, heading a moderate left-wing government.

Daoud was killed in 1978 in a Marxist coup. Nur Mohammad Taraki became president but was himself overthrown and killed in September 1979. Hafizullah Amin took over but was not to remain in power long.
In December 1979, Soviet troops landed in Kabul. They seized key buildings on December 27 and Babrak Karmal announced he had taken over the government. Hafizullah Amin was executed.

Karmal was replaced as general secretary (leader) of the ruling People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) by Najibullah in May 1986. Karmal resigned also as president later in November and Mohammad Tsamkani was made "caretaker" president.

Najibullah became president on September 30, 1987. A traditional government-convened "Loya Jirga" (grand assembly) in Kabul on November 29-30 adopted a new constitution and elected Najibullah president for seven years.

A guerrilla war pitting Soviet and Afghan government troops against Western-backed rebel forces began after the Soviet intervention. The U.N. General Assembly repeatedly voted for withdrawal of the Soviet troops and Afghanistan was suspended from the Organisation of Islamic Conference, which now consists of 54 nations.
From June 1982 a U.N. envoy conducted indirect talks between the Afghan and Pakistani governments to seek a solution to the conflict.

Despite the presence of some 115,000 Soviet troops in Afghanistan, the Mujahideen rebels continued to control much of the countryside, and the introduction of U.S.-made Stinger anti- aircraft missiles in 1987 swung the conflict in their favour.

In February 1988 Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and Najibullah announced that Soviet troops could withdraw by February 1989 if Afghanistan and Pakistan reached a settlement at the U.N.-mediated talks in Geneva.

In April 1988, Afghanistan, Pakistan, the Soviet Union and the United States signed an accord providing for Soviet withdrawal, a halt to outside help for the rebels, the return of the Afghan refugees and that Washington and Moscow should oversee and guarantee the plan.
In April 1992, rival guerrilla groups fought for control of Kabul and President Buhanuddin Rabbani emerged a victor but continued fighting killed 10,000 civilians in 1993.
Taleban Islamic militia emerged as a new force in October 1994 and since then have taken over most of Afghanistan, including the capital Kabul that was taken in September 1996.
Ousted president Rabbani fled northwards and formed an alliance with northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

A mutiny by Dostum's deputy and foreign minister General Abdul Malik on May 19, 1997, in collusion with the Taleban triggered the fall of opposition alliance strongholds in the north, including Dostum's capital of Mazar-i-Sharif and military headquarters Shibarghan.
